docs.title: Silo
docs.text:
A zero-configuration platform for publishing and collaboratively improving AI-generated applications.

Team (Group 3C75): Paras Kaushal (1024030984), Dev Kapla (1024030888), Devanshu (1024030876). Advisor: Dr. Nisha Thakur.

Upload a small app as a ZIP. Silo builds and runs it in Docker, lets the team edit its code together live in the browser, and checks every version for security risks before anyone trusts it.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
cd code
python scripts/start.py --local

Then open http://localhost:3000/auth/local. On Windows, double-click code/start-silo.bat. Requirements and options are in code/README.md.

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Devanshu’s Journal
docs.text:
Roll No. 1024030876 Name: Devanshu Area: Build System + Security Track

  • W1 : Build-inference engine
  • W2 : Docker builds and sample apps
  • W3 : Packaging engine for real projects
  • W4 : Build strategies and readiness check
  • W5 : Security analyser
  • W6 : Version comparison and Semgrep
  • W7 : Hidden-command detection and evaluation

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• Detection of language, Python version, entry file and port.
  • Dependency discovery from requirements.txt and import scanning.
  • Import-name to package-name map (93 entries) and standard-library filter.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: Fixed rules instead of an AI model, so deployment decisions are fast and predictable.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Silo works out how to run a Python project in under 2 ms.

docs.title: W2 : Docker builds and sample apps
What I built
docs.text:
• Dockerfile template (Jinja2) filled from the inferred plan.
  • Container start with an assigned port and resource limits.
  • Automatic fix of 127.0.0.1 to 0.0.0.0 in the build copy.
  • Five sample apps (Flask, FastAPI, Pandas, Streamlit, localhost app) with tests.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: Install dependencies before copying source, so Docker reuses cached layers.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: All five sample apps build and run.

docs.title: W3 : Packaging engine for real projects
What I built
docs.text:
• packaging.py: unwraps zip wrapper folders and picks the app folder in a monorepo.
  • Syntax-tree analysis to choose the start mode: uvicorn, gunicorn, Streamlit, Django or script.
  • Skips the project's own modules when resolving packages.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: Decide how to start the app, not just which file, so framework apps do not exit silently.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Real-world project layouts build, not only single-file apps.

docs.title: W4 : Build strategies and readiness check
What I built
docs.text:
• Three strategies in order: the project's Docker Compose file, its own Dockerfile, or a generated one.
  • Safe Compose: every path stays inside the project; no host volumes or networks.
  • A version is "live" only after the app answers HTTP.
  • PID lock files for crash recovery; Windows line-ending fix for scripts.
  • Static sites go live instantly without Docker.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: A running container is not proof; only a real HTTP response is.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: No more fake "live" apps; failed builds show their logs.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• security.py: Python rules on the syntax tree (shell commands, eval, pickle, SQL from strings, TLS off, debug mode, secrets).
  • JavaScript and HTML rules (innerHTML, tokens in localStorage, scripts without integrity).
  • Capability "nutrition label": files, network, commands, databases, web serving.
  • Risk score from 0 to 100; secret values masked.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: Findings come only from rules, never from AI, so results are repeatable.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Every version gets a label and a list of findings with fixes.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• Comparison of two versions: capabilities gained or lost, findings new or fixed, dependency changes.
  • Classification as Expanding or Reducing, with a plain-English summary.
  • Semgrep 1.183 alongside Silo's rules, with a disk cache.
  • Security Track API for the timeline, one version and "Fix with AI".

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: When both engines flag the same line, keep one finding, so nothing is counted twice.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Test case TC-03 passes: 10 problems found in v2, all fixed in v3 (risk 76 to 13).

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• Name resolver that traces renamed imports, importlib, __import__ and getattr to the real function.
  • Warning for module names built from pieces.
  • Regression tests; test apps for TC-03 and TC-04.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: Design TC-04 to fail first, then improve the analyser and show the difference.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: TC-04 passes: all three hidden commands found (risk 12 to 41).

docs.title: Dev’s Journal
docs.text:
Roll No. 1024030888 Name: Dev Kapla Area: Frontend

  • W1 : Frontend setup and design system
  • W2 : Home page and Dashboard
  • W3 : App Room
  • W4 : Workbench layout
  • W5 : Live editing in the browser
  • W6 : Security Track page
  • W7 : Polish and browser tests

docs.title: W1 : Frontend setup and design system
What I built
docs.text:
• Next.js 14 project with TypeScript and Tailwind CSS.
  • Design tokens in tailwind.config.ts: Silo colours, pill buttons, fonts.
  • Shared UI pieces: PillButton, Label, StatusDot, Modal, Drawer, Toast.
  • api.ts client and useAuth hook.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: Utility classes instead of separate CSS files, so every page looks consistent.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: A styled base that all later pages are built on.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• Landing page with sign-in, and local account sign-in.
  • Dashboard: scrolling banner, hero card for the latest app, app grid with search and filters, activity feed.
  • "+ New app" modal: name the app, drop a zip, upload in one step.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: Show each app as a preview card, not a row of technical details.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Users can see, search and create their apps.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• Full-screen live preview of the running app.
  • Version filmstrip to switch between versions.
  • Build drawer with real logs, polled while a build runs.
  • "Build details" panel: runtime, entry point, port, limits.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: The running app is the centre of the page; technical details open only on request.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Users watch a build finish and use their app straight away.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• Tool rail with drawers: Files, Comments, Changes, Timeline.
  • Preview with phone, tablet and desktop sizes.
  • AI and chat panel with the message composer and quick actions.
  • Proposal cards showing the AI's diff with Apply and Reject.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: One screen for preview, code, chat and AI, so users never switch pages.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The Workbench layout is complete, ready for live data.

docs.title: W5 : Live editing in the browser
What I built
docs.text:
• CodeMirror editor connected to Yjs (useCollaboration hook).
  • Other people's cursors and a presence list.
  • Status pill: Saving, Saved, Offline, "Access changed".
  • Share panel: invite links, roles, remove members, revoke links.
  • useWorkbench hook for checkpoints, preview and publish.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: Show "Saved" only after the server confirms the edit is stored.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Several people edit the same file at once and see each other live.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• Interactive build map with React Flow: one node per version, edges marked Expanding or Reducing.
  • Inspector panel: nutrition label, changes, findings, dependencies.
  • Finding cards with file, line, CWE, fix and "Fix with AI".
  • Capability matrix and risk-by-build chart.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: An interactive graph instead of static cards, so users explore versions by clicking.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Users see at a glance what each version can do and what changed.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• Playwright tests for collaboration, editor scrolling and the Security Track.
  • Automated evaluation test cases TC-01 to TC-04, with screenshots.
  • Separate build folders for the test and normal copies.
  • Layout and accessibility fixes across pages.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: Test with real browsers and separate accounts, not mocks.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: All 9 browser tests pass on the finished frontend.

docs.title: Paras’s Journal
docs.text:
Roll No. 1024030984 Name: Paras Kaushal Area: Backend + API

  • W1 : Backend foundation and database
  • W2 : Sign-in and app management
  • W3 : Uploads, versions and build logs
  • W4 : Collaboration data and sharing
  • W5 : Live editing server
  • W6 : AI collaborator
  • W7 : Local AI, launcher and testing

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• FastAPI project with uv for locked dependencies.
  • config.py: all settings read from .env into one object.
  • db.py and models.py: users, apps, versions and build logs (SQLAlchemy).
  • Alembic set up, with the first migration.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: Keep uploaded files outside the code folder, so the auto-reloader never restarts the API during a build.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The API starts, connects to PostgreSQL and creates its tables.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• Google OAuth sign-in, plus optional email and password accounts (PBKDF2 hashing).
  • Session as a signed JWT in an HttpOnly cookie.
  • Routes to create, list, rename and delete apps.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: One get_current_user_id dependency that every protected route uses.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Users sign in and manage their apps through the API.

docs.title: W3 : Uploads, versions and build logs
What I built
docs.text:
• POST /apps/{id}/versions: zip upload (8 MB limit) with zip-slip protection.
  • Each upload creates a numbered version in its own folder.
  • Builds start in a detached worker process; real logs are stored line by line.
  • On start-up, builds interrupted by a reboot are marked failed.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: Return immediately after upload and build in the background, so the page never waits.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Upload, build status and logs work end to end with the build system.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• Tables for drafts, checkpoints, comments, members, invites, releases and audit events (migration 0002).
  • Roles owner > editor > commenter > viewer, enforced by one app_access() function.
  • Invitation links: random, stored as a hash, 2-day expiry, revocable.
  • Checkpoints, restore, comments, preview and publish routes.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: Unknown apps return 404 instead of 403, so strangers cannot learn an app exists.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Everything the Workbench needs is available through the API.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• Node.js collaboration server with WebSockets and Yjs.
  • 15-minute tickets to join a room; viewers and commenters are read-only.
  • Every edit saved through the API before it is broadcast and confirmed.
  • Access re-checked every 5 seconds, so removed members are cut off.
  • Preview gateway that forwards to running apps after a ticket check.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: The database, not the WebSocket server, is the source of truth.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Two people can type on the same line and both changes are kept.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• POST /drafts/{id}/proposals: sends the request and code (without secret files) to Gemini.
  • Replies forced into a JSON patch, shown as a diff.
  • Apply only if the code has not changed since the AI read it.
  • Retries and fallback to lighter Gemini models when busy.
  • "Fix with AI" endpoint for Security Track findings.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: The AI only proposes; a person always reviews and applies.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Users ask for changes in plain English and review them before applying.

docs.title: W7 : Local AI, launcher and testing
What I built
docs.text:
• Local AI server running Gemma 4 E4B on the GPU (model and runtime on drive D).
  • Provider chain: local model first, Gemini when it is not running.
  • scripts/start.py and start-silo.bat: one command installs, starts and checks every part.
  • API test suite grown to 117 tests; clean code and README.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: Run the AI locally, so no code leaves the machine and no key is needed.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The finished backend is ready for evaluation and starts with a double-click.
